title: Correlation, Causation, and Confounding
editorial_note: Opening revised to lead with the lesson itself. Remaining dialogue is an automated editorial draft; review spoken wording and meaning before final publication.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Correlation, Causation, and Confounding.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Correlation describes variables varying together. Causation claims that intervening on one would change the other, all else relevant being equal. Prediction can be useful without causation, but product decisions usually involve intervention: if we build, prompt, require, or remove X, will Y change?

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at association is not intervention effect?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Confounding occurs when a common cause influences both the presumed cause and outcome. Reverse causation means the outcome or its precursor changes exposure. Selection bias appears when inclusion depends on variables related to both. Measurement changes, seasonality, regression to the mean, and simultaneous releases can create persuasive patterns.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Draw a causal diagram before controlling for variables. Include treatment, outcome, common causes, mediators through which treatment works, and selection. Controlling for every available field is unsafe: adjusting for a mediator can remove part of the effect; conditioning on a common effect can create a spurious association.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at match language to evidence?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Observational data supports “associated with” unless a credible causal design and assumptions justify stronger wording. Temporal order, a plausible mechanism, consistency, dose-response, comparison groups, and negative controls can strengthen an inference but do not automatically eliminate confounding.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Randomisation is powerful because assignment breaks expected dependence on pre-treatment causes. When experimentation is impossible or unethical, designs such as interrupted time series, difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity, matching, instrumental variables, or natural experiments may help—with specialist analysis and explicit assumptions.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: None is a magical label.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Qualitative research contributes mechanism and context. It can reveal why clinics update data and how that affects work, but it does not alone estimate causal magnitude.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Transfer example: help-widget use and retention
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: help-widget use and retention?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Customers who use a help widget renew more often. Heavy users may both encounter more questions and be more likely to renew. Forcing widget use could add friction rather than loyalty. Randomising a credible invitation estimates the effect of the invitation, not the effect of widget use among self-selecting users.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at where this can go wrong?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Post hoc story: a mechanism is invented after a chart moves. Control everything: mediators or colliders introduce bias. Predictive causality: model accuracy is mistaken for intervention evidence. Before/after certainty: time trends and concurrent changes are ignored. Selection blindness: only users who chose exposure are compared.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Aggregate reversal: segment composition drives the headline.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at make the causal model inspectable?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The diagram determines what to measure and what not to adjust away. Controlling for a mediator estimates a different question; adjusting for a variable caused by both exposure and outcome can introduce bias. Unmeasured confounding remains a limitation even when a regression includes many fields.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Predictive accuracy is not proof that changing the predictor will change the outcome.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The team combines design, natural variation, sensitivity analysis, negative controls where appropriate, and qualitative mechanism evidence. A randomised intervention can strengthen causal inference but may be unethical or suffer interference. Observational results use calibrated language and state population, timing, assumptions, and alternative explanations.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: premium support?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Customers using premium support may retain more because they are larger, have greater need, and receive more account attention. The correlation does not prove that offering support causes retention. A causal model identifies the selection and possible study designs.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where does the harder design decision appear?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Senior practitioners stop causal language from outrunning study design. They ask what changed besides the intervention, why units received exposure, whether groups were comparable before it, and which assumptions are untestable. They also distinguish the effect of offering, assigning, adopting, and complying—different questions that lead to different product decisions.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Draw the causal story before interpreting the number
turns.text: What changes when we look at draw the causal story before interpreting the number?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The team distinguishes prediction from intervention. Statistical control cannot repair unmeasured confounding or bad event definitions. Natural variation, experiments, and qualitative mechanism evidence strengthen inference, while results remain bounded to the population and conditions studied.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: <! -- Editorial: manual revision; curated product example --

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can we see that in a concrete product situation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Illustrative scenario: a retail app. People who use wish lists buy more often, but that does not prove wish lists cause buying. Committed shoppers may be more likely to save products in the first place. State the competing explanations, then choose an experiment or another design that can separate them before investing in a wish-list redesign.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should I notice the next time I use a product?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Find a claim that “users who do X are more likely to Y.” List three reasons people select into X, one reverse-causal story, and the intervention the claim quietly recommends. Does the evidence support that intervention?
